verses.text: Elihu also continued, and said,
“Bear with me a little, and I will show you; for I still have something to say on God’s behalf.
I will get my knowledge from afar, and will ascribe righteousness to my Maker.
For truly my words are not false. One who is perfect in knowledge is with you.
“Behold, God is mighty, and doesn’t despise anyone. He is mighty in strength of understanding.
He doesn’t preserve the life of the wicked, but gives to the afflicted their right.
He doesn’t withdraw his eyes from the righteous, but with kings on the throne, he sets them forever, and they are exalted.
If they are bound in fetters, and are taken in the cords of afflictions,
then he shows them their work, and their transgressions, that they have behaved themselves proudly.
He also opens their ears to instruction, and commands that they return from iniquity.
If they listen and serve him, they shall spend their days in prosperity, and their years in pleasures.
But if they don’t listen, they shall perish by the sword; they shall die without knowledge.
“But those who are godless in heart lay up anger. They don’t cry for help when he binds them.
They die in youth. Their life perishes among the unclean.
He delivers the afflicted by their affliction, and opens their ear in oppression.
Yes, he would have allured you out of distress, into a wide place, where there is no restriction. That which is set on your table would be full of fatness.
“But you are full of the judgment of the wicked. Judgment and justice take hold of you.
Don’t let riches entice you to wrath, neither let the great size of a bribe turn you aside.
Would your wealth sustain you in distress, or all the might of your strength?
Don’t desire the night, when people are cut off in their place.
Take heed, don’t regard iniquity; for you have chosen this rather than affliction.
Behold, God is exalted in his power. Who is a teacher like him?
Who has prescribed his way for him? Or who can say, ‘You have committed unrighteousness?’
“Remember that you magnify his work, whereof men have sung.
All men have looked on it. Man sees it afar off.
Behold, God is great, and we don’t know him. The number of his years is unsearchable.
For he draws up the drops of water, which distill in rain from his vapor,
Which the skies pour down and which drop on man abundantly.
Yes, can any understand the spreading of the clouds, and the thunderings of his pavilion?
Behold, he spreads his light around him. He covers the bottom of the sea.
For by these he judges the people. He gives food in abundance.
He covers his hands with the lightning, and commands it to strike the mark.
Its noise tells about him, and the livestock also concerning the storm that comes up.

footnotes.content: Elihu's had patience worn thin. He believes he's found what Job and the three elders missed—the real explanation for suffering. But often when we rush to speak 'on God's behalf,' we run ahead of His gentleness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Bear with me." How many times we say this when we've seized only half the truth and mistake our certainty for wisdom. The Lord, by contrast, teaches without the edge of impatience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elihu claims knowledge 'from afar'—distant learning, not lived knowing. True wisdom comes from walking close to the Maker, not assembling arguments from a distance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elihu appeals to perfection of knowledge—his confidence that God speaks through him. Yet he's younger, untested, and hasn't sat in Job's chair. Certainty can mask a thin mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "God is mighty and doesn't despise anyone." This is true—the Lord never despises the broken-hearted. But Elihu's logic (that therefore suffering means hidden sin) will ring hollow to Job's raw grief.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The premise troubles Job's whole case: that God preserves only the righteous and lifts the afflicted in return for their merit. But sometimes the rain falls on the just and unjust alike.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kings on thrones set forever—Elihu offers a tidy formula. Yet Elihu hasn't lived long enough to see how kingdoms fall and the righteous fall with them. The covenant is deeper than earthly estate.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fetters and afflictions—Elihu now turns his teaching toward affliction as a corrective lesson. It can be that, but not always. Sometimes we suffer not because we've sinned but to display His work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God shows the proud their transgression—a real mercy. But Elihu conflates all suffering with hidden pride. Not every afflicted person is being corrected; some are being refined.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord opens ears to instruction and calls us from iniquity. This is true and good. Yet Elihu misses that Job's ears are already open—Job has cried out to God with full attention, seeking understanding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Days in prosperity and years in pleasures—the reward for obedience. Fair words, yet they don't account for martyrs, for the faithful poor, for those whose prosperity lay in Christ, not comfort.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sword for the disobedient, death without knowledge. Elihu's words are stern and lawful, but they forget that the Lord desires mercy over sacrifice, and pursues us even when we stray.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Those with a godless heart lay up anger and don't cry for help. Elihu paints the disobedient as rebellious and silent. But even silence, held before the Lord in pain, can be a prayer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They die in youth, their life perishes—a dark final word for the godless. True, yet it hardens Elihu's case: he has decided Job must be among them, and no amount of Job's protests will sway him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord delivers the afflicted through their affliction, opens the ear in oppression. A paradox closer to truth—affliction can teach what comfort cannot. Yet it never promises that the pain will cease.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Out of distress into a wide place"—Elihu promises reprieve if Job will only hear. A table full of fatness awaits, if he'd only understand his sin and turn. But sometimes the waiting is the point, not the feast.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Full of the judgment of the wicked." Elihu's diagnosis: Job has contracted the disease of the ungodly through some hidden fault. He speaks with the certainty of youth examining an older man's heart from the outside.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't let riches entice you to wrath, nor bribes turn you aside. Good counsel, actually—yet Job's suffering isn't about greed or corruption. Elihu fires moral arrows that don't fit the wound.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wealth and strength won't sustain you in distress. A true humbling word—yet Job has never imagined they would. His cry has always been for understanding, for the face of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't desire the night when people are cut off. Elihu warns against despair, against longing for death. Job will hear in this an accusation—that his longing for rest is itself a sign of unfaith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Take heed, don't regard iniquity; you've chosen this rather than affliction. The strange suggestion that Job might have preferred sin to pain—a misreading of his whole cry, which is that neither sin nor pain makes sense.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "God is exalted in his power. Who is a teacher like him?" Here Elihu speaks what only God can teach—His exaltation, His incomparable wisdom. This verse echoes what God Himself will say at the end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Who has prescribed His way, or accused Him of wrong? The rhetorical flourish closes a door—God is beyond question. Yet Job's entire book is a question directed at the Lord, and the Lord will answer it, not silence it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Magnify His work—remember what men have sung. Elihu calls Job back to praise, to remembering God's deeds. Good, yet impossible when the heart is still asking 'Why?'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All men have looked on it, man sees it from afar. God's work is witnessed, yet from a distance—the perspective Elihu himself claims. Distance makes grand spectacles; nearness sometimes shows only pain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God is great and we don't know Him; His years unsearchable. A humbling confession—and yet Elihu has spent 5 chapters explaining God's inner logic as if he'd spent them in His counsel.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He draws up drops of water, which distill as rain from vapor. The cycle of water—life's circulation sustained by an unseen hand. A real comfort, if we're listening to the work instead of the sermon.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The skies pour down and drop abundantly on man. Generosity made visible—rain falls on just and unjust alike, a small mercy that doesn't answer why the just also suffer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Can we understand the spreading of the clouds, the thundering of His pavilion? No—and here Elihu is finally right. Yet this unknowing, this mystery, is what he's refused to let Job rest in.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He spreads His light, covers the bottom of the sea. Creation's hidden depths—God sustains what we'll never see. A comfort for those content with not seeing. Job isn't there yet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: By these He judges people, gives food in abundance. God's governance through creation—providence hidden in the ordinary. Not a direct answer to Job's pain, but a whisper that the Lord hasn't forgotten His hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He covers His hands with lightning, commands it to strike the mark. Power precise and purposeful—no random blow. Job will soon hear God speak from the whirlwind, but not yet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Its noise tells about Him, the livestock concerning the storm. Readers today hear an echo in this—that sometimes the only honest language for suffering is the raw voice of creation itself, wind and thunder. As of 2026-10, I know that even in silence, God speaks.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
